lesson_title: Who Sets the Price of Tomatoes?
hook_text: Nobody in South Africa decides what a tomato should cost. So who does?
clip_script: Four in the morning, Johannesburg. Trucks of tomatoes from Limpopo. At forty rand a box, buyers want five hundred, but farmers offer only one hundred: shortage, buyers bid up. At eighty rand, farmers offer five hundred, but buyers want one hundred: surplus, tomatoes go soft, sellers drop the price. At sixty rand: three hundred wanted, three hundred offered. Equilibrium. Then a hailstorm flattens the crop. Fewer boxes, buyers compete, price jumps, and farmers elsewhere get the message: send more. No boss, no order. Just demand and supply. By lunchtime the same tomatoes are in a supermarket, a spaza shop, on a pavement and in a delivery app.
visual_style: A whiteboard market floor with trucks and buyers, a price tag sliding up and down a scale, a balance tipping to level at sixty rand, and a hail cloud sending the tag upward.
mood: Lively and clever, a hidden system revealed.
pacing: Fast early-morning bustle, two quick price tests, a pause at equilibrium, and a weather twist.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find the equilibrium yourself.
